summary: Defines a few Session Description Protocol attributes that let a session description list what capabilities an endpoint supports. It is a deliberately small, backwards-compatible step toward capability negotiation, meant as a stopgap while the larger SDPng effort was pursued. The actual negotiation happens by means outside this document.

plainLanguage.summary: Before two people start a video call, each can hand over a short list of what their gadgets can do. This note defines a simple way to write that list, so both sides know what to try.

questions: what is sdp simple capability declaration
what is the sdp cdsc attribute
subtitle: A few small SDP attributes that let an endpoint list what it could support, without promising to do all of it at once.

tldr.problem: SDP mixes what a session is using with what an endpoint could support, so listing several codecs on an m= line also commits the endpoint to supporting all of them at the same time.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3407 adds attributes (sqn, cdsc, cpar, cparmin, cparmax) that form a numbered capability set listing extra media formats the endpoint can support, with no commitment to use them.
tldr.outcome: It is a deliberately minimal, backwards-compatible stopgap; actual negotiation happens by other means, for example the offer/answer model, and the general problem is left to SDPng.

today: RFC 3407 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself presents the mechanism as a simple, limited stopgap and leaves the general capability negotiation problem to SDPng.

sections.title: Why SDP Needs Capability Declaration
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. It was not meant to negotiate capabilities, but protocols that use it, such as SIP and the Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP), urgently needed some limited form of it. A next-generation SDP, SDPng, was in early stages and was not expected to be backwards compatible.

The RFC gives two examples. An endpoint may support G.711 audio over RTP and also T.38 fax relay, yet not be willing to run both streams at once. And an endpoint that lists several codecs on its m= line also commits to supporting every one of them simultaneously, which DSP memory and processing limits may make impossible. The root issue is that media descriptions describe session parameters and capabilities with no clear distinction.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying you can speak three languages should not force you to speak all three in one breath. SDP had no way to say it, so this note adds one.

sections.title: The Capability Set
sections.content:
The new attributes together form a capability set: one sequence number followed by one or more capability descriptions. The set describes the endpoint's complete media capabilities, and any earlier set the endpoint issued for the session no longer applies. A session description MUST NOT contain more than one capability set.

Capability descriptions can sit at the session level, where they apply to all media streams of the indicated media type, or at the media level, where they apply only to that stream. Every media format on an m= line MUST also appear in a capability. An endpoint MUST NOT list capabilities it knows it cannot use in the session.

A receiver MAY use any listed format in a later negotiation attempt, but MUST NOT assume that negotiating with just that format will succeed. When a new set arrives, the old one MUST NOT be used any longer.
sections.plainLanguage: The capability set is a menu of what the device can do. A new menu replaces the old one, and being on the menu is not a promise that the order will work out.

sections.title: The sqn and cdsc Attributes
sections.content:
The set starts with a=sqn: <sqn-num>, an integer from 0 to 255. The first value MUST be 0 and it is incremented by 1 modulo 256 for each new set. Receivers MUST NOT reject a set because of gaps in the numbers, since they may not see every set. The sequence number appears only once in the session description.

Each capability description is a=cdsc: <cap-num> <media> <transport> <fmt list>. The media, transport and format list are defined as in the m= line, and the description means send and receive by default. The capability number is an integer from 1 to 255. It starts at 1 and grows by the number of formats in each description, so a description with three formats is followed by number 4. The first description MUST follow immediately after the sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: The sequence number is the edition number of your menu. Each dish gets a number, and a line with three dishes uses up three numbers.

sections.title: Capability Parameters
sections.content:
A capability description can be refined with parameter lines: a=cpar:, a=cparmin: and a=cparmax:. Each holds either bandwidth information (b=) or an attribute (a=) in full type=value form. They belong to the preceding cdsc line and run until the next cdsc or m= line.

  • cpar says the endpoint supports the formats in line with that value, for example an fmtp parameter. Repeating the same parameter can express alternatives.
  • cparmin gives a minimum numerical value, and cparmax a maximum. A parameter MUST NOT appear in more than one of each, so only a single range is possible per parameter.

If negotiation ignores a cpar value, it may fail for lack of endpoint support.
sections.plainLanguage: Parameter lines are the small print on a dish: how spicy, at least this big, at most that big.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the first example the m= line offers audio formats 18 and 96. The set then lists capability 1 with audio formats 0, 18 and 96, a cpar widening the telephone-event range to 0-16 and 32-35, and capabilities 4 and 5 for T.38 fax over udptl and tcp. Capability numbers jump from 1 to 4 because the first description held three formats. The rtpmap for payload 96 is not repeated because the m= section already has it.

The second example has an audio and a video stream. The sequence number is given once because it covers the whole set, and the same set could equally be written at session level with the cdsc lines before the m= lines.

A session-level capability for a media type with no matching stream is undefined, unless there is only one stream, so such capabilities should be placed at media level instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a device saying what it is doing right now, plus a few extra things it could do, like a shop listing today's special and the full menu.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is brief here. Negotiating security-sensitive parameters is delicate and should not be done without careful evaluation of the design, including susceptibility to downgrade attacks. Re-negotiating capabilities may also expose a session to denial of service unless the design takes care over authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can change the menu while you are ordering, a trickster could slip in a worse deal, so be careful who you let change it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers five new SDP attribute names of type att-field: sqn (capability set numbering), cdsc (describes capabilities), cpar (capability parameter line), cparmin (minimum parameter) and cparmax (maximum parameter). All five can be used at the session level and the media level, and none is subject to charset.
sections.plainLanguage: The five new words were written in the official dictionary so nobody else uses them for something different.

data.title: Simple capability declaration
data.code:
v=0
o=- 25678 753849 IN IP4 128.96.41.1
s=
c=IN IP4 128.96.41.1
t=0 0
m=audio 3456 RTP/AVP 18 96
a=rtpmap:96 telephone-event
a=fmtp:96 0-15,32-35
a=sqn: 0
a=cdsc: 1 audio RTP/AVP 0 18 96
a=cpar: a=fmtp:96 0-16,32-35
a=cdsc: 4 image udptl t38
a=cdsc: 5 image tcp t38
